Chicken M'qualli with Preserved Lemon

Moroccan · Medium · Serves 4–6

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
M'qualli — the golden, saffron-perfumed chicken of the Moroccan canon — is the tagine's first lesson and its foundation: chicken on the bone, colored and scented with saffron and ginger, cooked gently with onions that melt into its own sauce, and finished with the two ingredients that make it unmistakably itself — preserved lemon (#92) and the brine-cured green olives. It is the dish every Moroccan household cooks and every visitor remembers, and it is this site's master record for the tagine canon that follows: the slow pot, the steam's patience, the preserved-lemon finish.

- **Marinate the chicken 1 hour in half of everything.** The saffron water, garlic, fresh ginger, spices, and a pinch of salt massaged into the pieces — the tagine's head start, its seasoning driven inward before the pot begins. The second half of the spice measure joins at the cooking. - **The bridge:** preserved lemons are the recipe's soul — they are a month's craft or a jar from any Middle Eastern grocer, and this site's #92 carries the making. The olives bridge with any good cracked green olive, blanched; the saffron is the one extravagance, and #120's steeping note is its law.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The marinade: an hour, saffron forward, driven inward.
  • The simmer: half-height liquid, the barest tremble, onions dissolved to sauce.
  • The finish: peel off the flame, butter's gloss, the ten-minute rest.

Chicken M'qualli with Preserved Lemon

Prep: 30 minutes, plus 1 hour marinating · Cook: 1 hour · Total: About 2 hours 30 minutes · Serves 4–6

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 1 whole chicken (about 1.6 kg), cut in 8 pieces, or 1.2 kg bone-in thighs
  • 1 large onion (about 200 g), grated or sliced paper-thin (the grated melts to sauce; the sliced gives texture — both honest)
  • 4 cloves garlic (about 15 g), grated; 1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated (about 10 g)
  • 1 tsp saffron threads (about 1 g), steeped 10 minutes in 3 tbsp hot water (#120)
  • 2 tsp ground ginger; 1 tsp turmeric; 1 tsp white pepper; ½ tsp cinnamon (the quiet register)
  • 1 preserved lemon (#92), quartered — the pulp to the pot, the peel sliced to finish
  • 150 g green olives, cracked (the bitter-cured Moroccan style), blanched 2 minutes to tame
  • 3 tbsp olive oil (about 40 g); 1 tsp salt; a fist of cilantro and parsley (about 30 g), tied
  • Water or stock, 250 ml (approximately); butter (about 20 g) and a handful more cilantro to finish

Instructions

  1. **The pot's beginning (10 minutes).** In the tagine, Dutch oven, or wide heavy pot, warm the oil and add the marinated chicken pieces, turning to coat and lightly gold at the edges — 4 minutes a side, no crowd, in batches if the pot runs small. Add the onion, the remaining spices, and the herb bundle; stir 2 minutes to the pot's perfume. Checkpoint — the pot's base should smell of saffron and ginger over browning chicken, the onion just beginning to wilt. This is not a sear; it is a coating — the color comes from saffron and turmeric, and the gold at the edges is enough.
  2. **The covered simmer (45 minutes at the tremble).** Add the preserved lemon's pulp, the blanched olives, and the water — the liquid should barely reach half the chicken's height, because the tagine's sauce is the bird's own condensation, not a bath. Cover, adjust to the barest simmer (roughly 95 °C, one bubble at a time), and cook 40–45 minutes, turning the pieces once, until the chicken is tender to the bone and the onions have dissolved into a shallow, golden, spoon-coating sauce. Checkpoint — at 45 minutes: the chicken should yield at the bone's twist, the sauce a scant inch of gold silk — thicker than broth, far less than a stew, and glossy with the rendered chicken fat and saffron's oil. Taste: the salt should be one notch under final (the lemon peel comes). If the sauce runs thin, uncover and simmer 5 minutes to reduce; if the pot runs dry, a splash of water — the tagine's mercy.
  3. **The finish — the preserved-lemon law (5 minutes off the flame).** Off the heat: the preserved lemon's peel, sliced to threads, stirred through and left to steep 5 minutes; the butter swirled in to gloss, the fresh cilantro over. Rest the pot 10 minutes before serving — the sauce's final thickening is the rest, and the lemon peel's perfume needs it. Checkpoint — eating test, over couscous or bread: the chicken's saffron-gold flesh, tender to the bone's edge and seasoned through — the sauce's ginger-warm silk beneath, and then the preserved lemon's arrival at the swallow: salt, fermentation's depth, and a floral-bitter brightness that no fresh lemon on earth delivers. The olives' brine-cured chew runs between. It should taste like the canon's foundation — a dish whose every element the next thirty tagines on this site will rearrange.

Finish & Plate

The pot to the table's center — the chicken fanned in its gold inch of sauce, the lemon threads and olives visible, cilantro over — with couscous (#34), khobz for the sopping, or the #75's vegetables beside. The second day's reheated pot, the lemon steeped overnight, is the canon's open secret.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Sauce thin, wateryLiquid over-measured or lid ajarHalf-height water; uncover to reduce at the end
Chicken dryBoiled, not trembledThe 95 °C law; pull at the bone's yield
Lemon's perfume absentPeel boiled in the potThe peel goes in off the flame, always

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- Keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves overnight (the lemon's steep — the canon's law); the chicken, picked from the bone, becomes the #21 batbout's filling or the #38 pastilla's meat. The sauce freezes 2 months as the canon's mother-stock. - Variations: the beef and lamb clocks (longer, same doctrine), the #42 chtitha's fierce sister. This record is the canon's master; the #40 djej bil zaytoun is its olive-forward sibling, and the preserved lemon's own record is #92.
